body:
Meaning of weathering

Rocks formed deep within the Earth or under earlier geological conditions may become unstable when exposed to atmospheric gases, surface water, temperature variations and living organisms. These influences gradually break down or alter the rock.

Weathering is the physical disintegration and chemical decomposition of rocks at or near the Earth's surface, occurring essentially in place.

The term in situ means that the rock is broken down or altered at its original location. Weathering does not require substantial transportation of rock fragments by an external agent.

The loose and altered material produced by weathering may contribute to a surface layer called the regolith. Some of this material may later develop into soil, while some may be removed by erosion or mass movements.

Weathering, erosion and mass wasting

These processes often operate together, but they perform different roles in the transformation of the Earth's surface.

ProcessMain actionExample
WeatheringBreakdown or alteration in placeRock cracked by freezing water
ErosionRemoval of earth material by moving agentsRunning water removing sediment
TransportationMovement of removed materialRiver carrying suspended silt
Mass wastingDownslope movement mainly under gravityRockfall or landslide
DepositionAccumulation of transported materialSediment settling in a river basin

The distinction is particularly important between erosion by a transporting agent and mass wasting driven directly by gravity. A mass movement may contain water, but running water need not be the agent carrying the material.

The combined lowering and wearing away of the Earth's surface through weathering, erosion and mass movements is broadly called denudation.

The 3 major categories of weathering

  • Physical or mechanical weathering: Breaks rocks into smaller pieces without fundamentally changing the chemical composition of their minerals.
  • Chemical weathering: Dissolves minerals or changes their chemical composition through reactions involving water, gases or other substances.
  • Biological weathering: Results from the activities of living organisms and may involve physical breakdown, chemical decomposition or both.

These categories are not mutually exclusive in nature. For example, a growing plant root can widen an existing crack mechanically, while organic acids associated with biological activity can chemically alter the minerals exposed within that crack.

Factors controlling the rate of weathering

Climate

Temperature and moisture strongly influence weathering. Warm, humid conditions generally favour chemical and biological weathering. Repeated freezing and thawing favours frost action where water is available. Large temperature variations and evaporation can encourage mechanical weathering in dry regions.

Mineral composition

Some minerals are more resistant to alteration than others. Quartz is relatively resistant to many ordinary chemical weathering processes, while calcite dissolves comparatively readily in weakly acidic water.

Rock structure

Joints, fractures and bedding planes provide pathways through which water, air and roots can penetrate. A highly fractured rock may therefore weather more rapidly than an otherwise similar intact rock.

Relief, vegetation and time

Slope influences drainage, exposure and the removal of weathered material. Vegetation can accelerate chemical and biological alteration while protecting the ground from some forms of erosion. Longer exposure generally allows greater cumulative weathering, although rates vary with local conditions.

Differential weathering

When neighbouring rocks or minerals weather at different rates, the resulting process is called differential weathering. Resistant rocks may remain as raised features while less resistant materials are preferentially removed by erosion.

For example, hard quartzite beds in parts of northern and northeastern Gujarat can form prominent ridges, while less resistant surrounding rock formations weather and erode more readily.

Prelims focus

  • Weathering is essentially an in-situ process.
  • Erosion involves removal of material.
  • Mass wasting is driven directly by gravity.
  • Chemical weathering is generally favoured by warm, moist conditions.
  • Rock fractures increase opportunities for weathering agents to penetrate.
  • Trap: Weathering and erosion are related processes but are not synonyms.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Geomorphic Processes, Weathering and Exogenic Processes, online chapter available through SATHEE and Philoid; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, 2018-19 reprint, Chapter 2, p. 13; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 7, Landforms; US National Park Service, Weathering; V. N. Kulkarni, Geology of Gujarat, Navnirman, July-December 1985. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Weathering, Erosion and the Factors Controlling Rock Breakdown

body:
Mechanical disintegration of rocks

Physical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces through mechanical forces. The fragments generally retain the original mineral composition, although their size, shape and exposed surface area change.

Mechanical breakdown is particularly important because it creates additional surfaces on which water, oxygen and other chemical agents can act.

Thermal expansion and contraction

Rocks expand when heated and contract when cooled. Different minerals within the same rock may expand and contract by different amounts. The outer part of a rock may also experience temperature changes more rapidly than its interior.

Repeated temperature variations produce stresses that may gradually loosen mineral grains or enlarge existing cracks.

  • Granular disintegration: Individual mineral grains become detached, causing the rock surface to crumble.
  • Block disintegration: A rock breaks into relatively large blocks, commonly along existing joints or fractures.
  • Exfoliation: Curved or sheet-like outer layers detach from a rock surface.

Thermal weathering is important in regions with substantial temperature variations, including many arid environments. Its effectiveness also depends on rock properties and exposure conditions.

Freeze-thaw weathering or frost action

Water enters joints and cracks in rocks. When the temperature falls below freezing, ice formation and associated pressure can enlarge these cracks. Water increases in volume by approximately 9% when it freezes under ordinary conditions.

When the ice melts, water can penetrate farther into the enlarged openings. Repeated freezing and thawing gradually weakens the rock and may detach angular fragments. This mechanism is also known as frost wedging.

Frost weathering is particularly effective where temperatures repeatedly fluctuate around the freezing point and liquid water is available, such as many high mountain and cold-climate environments.

Extremely low temperatures alone do not necessarily produce maximum freeze-thaw weathering. Repeated changes between freezing and thawing, together with sufficient moisture, are important.

Pressure release and unloading

Rocks formed at considerable depths are subjected to pressure from the weight of overlying materials. When erosion removes these materials, the pressure on the underlying rock decreases.

This unloading may allow the exposed rock to expand and develop fractures broadly parallel to its surface. Successive detachment of curved sheets can produce rounded rock masses and exfoliation domes, particularly in massive rocks such as granite.

Exfoliation describes the resulting separation of surface sheets. It can arise from unloading, thermal stresses and other mechanical processes; it is not restricted to a single cause.

Salt crystallisation

Water containing dissolved salts can enter rock pores and cracks. When the water evaporates, salt crystals grow within these confined spaces. Continued crystal growth may exert pressure on the surrounding rock and progressively damage it.

Salt weathering is common in arid and semi-arid areas where evaporation is strong, as well as in coastal environments where rocks are exposed to saline water or sea spray.

Salt crystallisation is classified as mechanical weathering when the growth of crystals physically breaks the rock. This is distinct from chemical weathering in which the original rock minerals undergo dissolution or alteration.

Wetting and drying

Some clay-rich materials swell when they absorb water and shrink when they dry. Repeated swelling and shrinkage can produce cracks and weaken clay-rich rocks and weathered deposits.

This mechanism contributes to mechanical deterioration in environments that alternate between wet and dry seasons.

Importance of physical weathering

Mechanical weathering produces rock debris, helps develop regolith and increases the area available for chemical reactions. It can also loosen rock masses on steep slopes, making them more susceptible to rockfalls and other mass movements.

Prelims focus

  • Mechanical weathering does not fundamentally change mineral chemistry.
  • Water expands by approximately 9% on freezing.
  • Frost action is favoured by repeated freezing and thawing.
  • Unloading can produce sheet fractures and exfoliation domes.
  • Salt crystallisation is important in dry and saline coastal environments.
  • Trap: A process involving dissolved salts may still be mechanical if crystal growth is responsible for breaking the rock.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Geomorphic Processes, Physical Weathering Processes and Exfoliation; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 7, pp. 46-48; US National Park Service, Weathering, and Acadia National Park, Physical and Chemical Weathering educational material. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Physical Weathering: Temperature, Frost, Pressure Release and Salt Action

body:
Chemical weathering

Chemical weathering alters or dissolves the minerals within rocks. Water is a major agent because it can dissolve substances, transport dissolved gases and participate directly in chemical reactions.

Oxygen, carbon dioxide and acids derived from biological activity also contribute to chemical weathering. Many reactions proceed more rapidly under warm, moist conditions because both water availability and temperature influence reaction rates.

Major chemical weathering processes

Solution or dissolution

Some minerals dissolve when they come into contact with water. Rock salt is readily soluble, while minerals such as gypsum have more limited but significant solubility.

Water can remove soluble mineral constituents from a rock without first breaking the entire rock into fragments. Continued dissolution may enlarge pores and fractures.

Carbonation

Carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and soil dissolves in water and produces weak carbonic acid. This weakly acidic water reacts with carbonate minerals such as calcite.

The essential reactions can be represented as:

CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3

CaCO3 + H2CO3 ⇌ Ca2+ + 2HCO3−

Carbonation is particularly important in limestone regions. Carbonated water can enlarge joints in limestone and contribute to the development of underground cavities and karst landscapes.

Marble, although a metamorphic rock, is also susceptible to dissolution where it consists predominantly of calcite. Susceptibility to chemical weathering therefore depends on mineral composition, not merely the rock family.

Oxidation

Oxidation occurs when minerals react with oxygen or undergo related electron-transfer reactions. Iron-bearing minerals commonly undergo oxidation in the presence of oxygen and moisture, producing iron oxides and related compounds.

These compounds frequently impart reddish, brownish or yellowish colours to weathered rocks and soils. A dark iron-bearing rock such as basalt may consequently develop a reddish-brown weathered surface.

Reduction

Reduction may occur under conditions of limited oxygen, especially in poorly drained or waterlogged soils and sediments. Changes in the oxidation state of iron can increase its mobility and contribute to greyish or greenish colours.

Oxidation and reduction are influenced by drainage conditions and oxygen availability.

Hydration

Hydration occurs when water becomes incorporated into the structure of a mineral. The process may produce a new hydrated mineral and cause an increase in volume, weakening the surrounding rock.

For example, anhydrite can combine with water to form gypsum.

Hydrolysis

Hydrolysis involves chemical reactions between water and minerals that alter the original mineral structure. Feldspar and other silicate minerals may undergo hydrolysis and form clay minerals together with dissolved constituents.

The formation of clay through silicate weathering is an important step in soil development.

ProcessCharacteristic changeExample
SolutionMineral dissolvesRock salt in water
CarbonationReaction with carbonated waterLimestone dissolution
OxidationOxidation of mineral constituentsIron oxide formation
ReductionAlteration under oxygen-poor conditionsIron changes in waterlogged soil
HydrationWater incorporated into mineral structureAnhydrite to gypsum
HydrolysisWater reacts with mineral constituentsFeldspar alteration to clay minerals

Biological weathering

Living organisms influence rocks through mechanical activity and through the production of chemically active substances.

  • Plant roots: Roots penetrate existing fractures and may enlarge them as they grow.
  • Burrowing animals: Earthworms, termites and other organisms disturb surface materials and improve access for air and water.
  • Lichens and microorganisms: Their biological activity can release substances that gradually alter exposed mineral surfaces.
  • Decomposing organic matter: Decomposition produces carbon dioxide and organic acids that can accelerate mineral alteration.

Interaction between physical and chemical weathering

Physical breakdown exposes additional mineral surfaces, allowing chemical reactions to proceed over a greater area. Chemical alteration can in turn weaken minerals and the bonds between grains, making mechanical disintegration easier.

Biological activity frequently assists both processes. Weathering therefore normally involves a combination of mechanisms, although one mechanism may dominate under particular climatic or geological conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Dissolved carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid in water.
  • Carbonation is important in limestone dissolution.
  • Oxidation of iron-bearing minerals commonly produces reddish or brownish weathering products.
  • Hydration involves incorporation of water; hydrolysis involves chemical reaction with water.
  • Weathering of feldspar can produce clay minerals.
  • Trap: Biological weathering may be mechanical, chemical or a combination of both.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Geomorphic Processes, Chemical Weathering Processes and Biological Activity and Weathering; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 7, pp. 46-48; US National Park Service, Weathering and Weathering and Erosion; British Geological Survey, educational material on weathering. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
